# Dependenies & Preparation

First we import the required libraries and set up the paths.
We also assume that the `coderdata` package is installed and available in the Python environment and that we have downloaded the most recent coderdata dataset.

This can be done with the following command in the terminal:
```bash
coderdata download --local_path PATH_TO_SAVE_DATASET
```
Additionally we will use `reticulate` to interface with Python from R.

```{r}
#| label: imports-and-setup
#| warning: false

# r libraries
library(reticulate)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)

# path setup
data_dir <- "/tmp/coderdata/data/"

# defines the python environment to use
py_require("coderdata")

# import the coderdata package from python
cd <- import("coderdata")
```

Once we have loaded the `coderdata` package, we can check the version and list the available datasets to confirm that we have the correct version and datasets available.
```{r}
#| label: confirm-version-and-datasets
cd$version()
cd$list_datasets()
```

# Data import
Now we are ready to load the datasets and format them for analysis. We will load the `ccle` and `ctrpv2` datasets and format them to extract the relevant metrics for our analysis.
Note how this is done using the `reticulate` functionality to call Python functions from R via `cd$load(...)` and `datasets[[name]]$format(...)`.

```{r}
#| label: load-datasets
#| warning: false


datasetnames <- c("ccle", "ctrpv2", "nci60", "prism", "gdscv1", "gdscv2", "fimm")
datasets <- list()

for (name in datasetnames) {
  datasets[[name]] <- cd$load(name, local_path = data_dir)
}

experiments <- list()
for (name in datasetnames) {
  experiments[[name]] <- datasets[[name]]$format(
    "experiments",
    shape = "wide",
    metrics = c("auc", "fit_auc", "fit_r2")
  )
}
```

We also perform some basic data cleaning to remove any rows with invalid values for the metrics of interest. We will filter the datasets to only include rows where the `fit_auc`, `auc`, and `fit_r2` values are between 0 and 1.


```{r}
#| label: filter-datasets
#| 
dfs <- list()
for (name in datasetnames) {
  dfs[[name]] <- experiments[[name]] %>%
    .[
      .$fit_auc >= 0 &
      .$fit_auc <= 1 &
      .$auc >= 0 &
      .$auc <= 1 &
      .$fit_r2 >= 0 &
      .$fit_r2 <= 1,
    ]
}

head(dfs[['ccle']])
```

For the sake of transparency, we will also report the number of rows that were removed from each dataset during the filtering process. This will help us understand the impact of the filtering on the datasets and ensure that we are not losing too much information.
```{r}
#| label: report-filtering
for (name in datasetnames) {
  original_rows <- nrow(experiments[[name]])
  filtered_rows <- nrow(dfs[[name]])
  removed_rows <- original_rows - filtered_rows
  cat(paste0("Dataset: ", name, " - Original rows: ", original_rows, ", Filtered rows: ", filtered_rows, ", Removed rows: ", removed_rows, "\n"))
}
```

# Generating the figure(s)

## Defining the plotting function

For the figure, we will create a multi-panel plot that shows the relationships between the metrics of interest.
We will create scatter plots for `fit_auc` vs `auc` and `fit_auc` vs `fit_r2`, along with marginal histograms for each of the metrics.

In order to be able to reuse the plotting code for different datasets, we are defining a function `generate_figure()` that takes a dataframe and a dataset name as input and returns a combined plot object. To achieve this we are going to make use of the `patchwork` package to create a multi-panel figure that shows the relationships between the metrics of interest. We will create scatter plots for `fit_auc` vs `auc` and `fit_auc` vs `fit_r2`, along with marginal histograms for each of the metrics. To that end we first generate the individual plots and then combine them later on into a single figure using the `patchwork` package.

Once all of the plot objects have been created, we can combine them into a single figure using the `patchwork` package. We will use the `plot_layout()` function to specify the layout of the plots and the `area()` function to define the areas for each plot.

```{r}
#| label: generate-figure

generate_figure <- function(df, dataset_name) {
  p_main_auc <- ggplot(df, aes(x = auc, y = fit_auc)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
    geom_density2d() +
    labs(
      x = "AUC",
      y = "Fit AUC"
    ) +
    xlim(0, 1) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    theme_minimal()

  p_main_r2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = fit_r2, y = fit_auc)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
    geom_density2d() +
    labs(
      x = "Fit R2",
      y = "Fit AUC"
    ) +
    xlim(0, 1) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    theme_minimal()

  p_margin_left <- ggplot(df, aes(x = auc)) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", bins = 30) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

  p_margin_top_auc <- ggplot(df, aes(x = fit_auc)) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", bins = 30) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

  p_margin_top_r2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = fit_r2)) +
    geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", bins = 30) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

  layout <- c(
  area(t = 1, l = 2, b = 1, r = 3), # Top marginal (auc)
  area(t = 1, l = 4, b = 1, r = 5), # Top marginal (r2)
  area(t = 2, l = 1, b = 3, r = 1), # Left marginal (fit_auc)
  area(t = 2, l = 2, b = 3, r = 3), # Main plot auc)
  area(t = 2, l = 4, b = 3, r = 5) # Main plot (fit_r2)
)

  # plot(layout)
  plot <- p_margin_top_auc +
    p_margin_top_r2 +
    p_margin_left +
    p_main_auc +
    p_main_r2 +
    plot_layout(
      design = layout,
      widths = c(1, 4, 1),
      heights = c(1, 4),
      axes = 'collect_y'
    ) + 
    plot_annotation(title = paste("Dataset:", dataset_name))

  plot
}

```

## Combined dataset plot

```{r}
#| label: combine-datasets
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig.cap: "Figure 1: Multi-panel plot showing the relationships between AUC, Fit AUC, and Fit R2 for the combined datasets."

df_combined <- do.call(rbind, dfs)
df_plot <- df_combined[sample(nrow(df_combined), 100000), ]
plot <- generate_figure(df_plot, "Combined Datasets")
plot
```

## Generating the plots for each dataset

Now that the function to generate the figure has been defined, we can use it to create the plots for each dataset. We will store the plots in a list and then print them one by one.

```{r}
#| label: generate-plots

plots <- list()
for (name in names(dfs)) {
  plots[[name]] <- generate_figure(dfs[[name]], name)
}

```

Now we can print the plots for each dataset. This will display the multi-panel figures for each dataset, allowing us to visually compare the relationships between the metrics of interest across the different datasets.

```{r}
#| label: print-plot-ccle
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 6
#| fig.align: center
#| fig.cap: "Figure 2: Multi-panel plot showing the relationships between AUC, Fit AUC, and Fit R2 for the CCLE dataset."

print(plots[["ccle"]])
```

## Saving the plots to disk
Finally we save the plots to disk as PNG files.

```{r}
#| label: save-plots
#| warning: false
#| eval: false

for (name in names(plots)) {
  ggsave(filename = paste0("figure_1_", name, ".png"), plot = plots[[name]], width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
}

```
